idiom_name: policy as a type parameter constrained by an interface
implementation_notes: Go's generics can parameterize a type on a policy type (type Cache[K comparable, V any, P Evictor[K]] struct { policy P }), and because interfaces are satisfied structurally the policy only has to provide the declared methods - but constraint interfaces are the entire contract, generic code may call nothing beyond them, and Go has no policy inheritance, no extension mechanism conditioned on a type parameter and (even after generic methods arrived in Go 1.27) no generic interface methods. Enrichment and graceful degradation are therefore impossible: the classic structure must be hand-built, and shared behaviour has to be free functions taking the host. For most Go code an interface-typed field chosen at construction (Strategy) or functional options is the honest idiom; bind a policy as a type parameter only when the choice must be fixed at compile time and the code is genuinely hot.
pitfalls: The constraint interface is the whole contract: a policy with additional capabilities is unusable and the host cannot discover optional members, so there is no graceful degradation.

Constraint interfaces must be declared where the host can name them; a type whose method set merely resembles the policy does not satisfy a constraint unless the method signatures match exactly (pointer receivers included).

Each type-argument set instantiates its own generic code, so unbounded policy types inflate binaries and build times; storing the policy as a plain interface value instead re-adds itab dispatch without the compile-time guarantee.
